title: The badge in two places
objectives: Construct a parenthesized OR inside an event-type boundary.
Filter failure actions without equating failure with malicious intent.
story: MIDNIGHT AT MERIDIAN / CHAPTER 2 — Jules produces a cue sheet: his job was lighting, not donations. Meanwhile the shared publishing account appears on a support ticket and in an access review. The same account name can describe someone acting or something being acted on. Before blaming the badge holder, follow both roles and keep every alternative inside the login question.

teaching.heading: Actor is not a job title
teaching.text: Principal describes an actor in an event. Target describes the affected or referenced thing. Neither means CEO, engineer or administrator. Your source's mapping decides what the fields contain.

teaching.heading: AND narrows; OR offers alternatives
teaching.text: A AND B requires both. A OR B permits either. To ask for login events involving either identity role, keep the identity alternatives inside parentheses.

teaching.heading: Read the whole question
teaching.text: Category AND (principal OR target) keeps both branches inside the login category. Category AND principal OR target can let the final branch escape that category.

teaching.heading: The query is a lead
teaching.text: A failure record does not prove an attack. Use context and chronology privately. The course only checks whether the query asks its stated question.

teaching.heading: Follow evidence across roles
teaching.text: A pivot means taking one lead, such as an account, and asking a new scoped question about it. A match tells you where the identifier appears. Read the event category and principal/target roles before deciding what the person did.

challenges.title: Follow either identity role
challenges.prompt: Select only USER_LOGIN events in which [USER] appears in principal.user.userid OR target.user.userid. Preserve the event-type requirement for both branches. Use exact case-sensitive strings and return event rows.
hints: The category must constrain every identity branch.
Place the two identity alternatives inside parentheses, then AND that group with USER_LOGIN.

methodQuestions.prompt: What do the parentheses around the two identity alternatives preserve?

options.label: Only the principal alternative requires USER_LOGIN.
The USER_LOGIN requirement applies to either identity match.
The two identity fields must both match.

methodQuestions.rationale: AND (principal OR target) applies the event category to both alternatives.

methodQuestions.prompt: What changes if OR between the identity fields becomes AND?

options.label: Either identity field can still match independently.
The query searches two records and joins them.
Both identity fields must match the symbol in the same record.

methodQuestions.rationale: AND narrows the same-record filter. It is not a cross-event join.

mission.beat: The same publishing account appears in login records as actor or target. Jules asks, 'Does my name appearing mean I did it?' Search either role, but keep both alternatives inside USER_LOGIN.

explanation.meaning: The account recorded in the actor role specified by this query.
The account in the affected or referenced role. Check source meaning privately.
Permit either identity field to match the same course symbol.
Require the login category for both alternatives. Parentheses keep that boundary intact.

mission.remember: OR opens alternatives. Parentheses keep the doorframe.
mission.caseUpdate: Case clue: an access review mentions the account as the object being checked, not necessarily the operator. Role and event category matter before attribution.

analystNote.text: In UDM, principal generally describes the acting entity and target the entity acted upon. The same identifier in a different role can tell a different story. Check the source mapping and event context.

challenges.title: Keep the failure question focused
challenges.prompt: Select USER_LOGIN events with security_result.action = FAIL and principal.user.userid exactly [USER]. No target-role OR is requested in this challenge. Return event rows.
hints: Keep category and exact actor identity, then add the documented action filter.
Use security_result.action = "FAIL" as another required condition.

methodQuestions.prompt: What happens if the account condition is removed from this failed-login query?

options.label: It can return failed-login records for other accounts.
It includes successful logins for that account.
It changes the failure action into a text search.

methodQuestions.rationale: Removing the account constraint broadens account scope while retaining USER_LOGIN and FAIL.

methodQuestions.prompt: What changes if the three conditions are joined with OR instead of AND?

options.label: Every record must still satisfy all three conditions.
A record can match any one condition, broadening the search.
Only the most specific condition is used.

methodQuestions.rationale: OR accepts alternatives. A FAIL action or an account match could admit records outside the intended combined scope.

mission.beat: Mira now wants only failed logins where the publishing account is the principal. The broader two-role query answered an earlier question; narrow it deliberately.

explanation.meaning: Require the stated actor account, using only the training symbol here.
All three requirements must hold together.

mission.remember: A narrow question needs every boundary attached.
mission.caseUpdate: Case clue: the support team confirms old credentials were tried during setup. That is a plausible explanation to test, not permission to ignore other access. The next lead is the publishing workstation.

analystNote.text: Keeping the right role, account and event category limits unrelated matches. A broad OR can produce convincing-looking records that never satisfied the account question.
